subject: Geography
sub_topic: Types of rocks — igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic

concepts.name: Classification of Igneous Rocks: Intrusive vs. Extrusive
key_dimensions: Mechanism of formation: cooling rate and crystal size relationship (trap for UPSC — slow cooling = large crystals, fast = fine/glassy)
Intrusive types: plutonic (batholiths, laccoliths, sills, dykes) vs. extrusive types: lava flows, pyroclastic rocks
Texture differences: phaneritic vs. aphanitic vs. glassy (obsidian) — frequently confused in MCQs
Geographic examples: Deccan Traps (extrusive basalt) vs. granite batholiths of Aravalli — India-specific traps

concepts.name: Intrusive Igneous Landforms: Batholiths, Laccoliths, Sills, and Dykes
key_dimensions: Definitional precision: concordant (parallel to rock strata — sills, laccoliths) vs. discordant (cuts across strata — dykes, batholiths) — classic UPSC trap
Scale and exposure: batholiths exposed after denudation form inselbergs/domes; laccoliths form dome-shaped hills
Dykes as resistant ridges after differential erosion — geomorphic outcome linkage
India examples: Rajasthan dykes, Karnataka granite batholiths — map-based question relevance

concepts.name: Volcanic Extrusive Rocks: Basalt and Rhyolite — Properties and Landform Association
key_dimensions: Basalt: low silica, low viscosity, mafic composition — forms shield volcanoes and lava plateaus (Deccan Plateau)
Rhyolite: high silica, high viscosity, felsic — forms explosive volcanoes, calderas
Columnar jointing in basalt (e.g., Giant's Causeway concept) — process and landform link
Trap between basalt and granite: both igneous but basalt is extrusive fine-grained, granite is intrusive coarse-grained

concepts.name: The Rock Cycle: Interconversion Pathways and Conditions
key_dimensions: Directional flow: igneous → sedimentary (weathering + deposition), sedimentary → metamorphic (heat/pressure), metamorphic → igneous (melting)
Reverse pathways: metamorphic rocks can be re-melted into magma — often overlooked in MCQs
Role of plate tectonics in driving the rock cycle (subduction melts rocks → magma)
UPSC trap: sedimentary rocks can directly become igneous without becoming metamorphic first if melted

concepts.name: Formation of Sedimentary Rocks: Processes of Lithification and Diagenesis
key_dimensions: Sequential process: weathering → erosion → transportation → deposition → compaction → cementation (lithification)
Diagenesis vs. metamorphism: diagenesis at low temperature/pressure (sedimentary stage) vs. metamorphism at high T/P — boundary often tested
Types of cementing agents: silica, calcite, iron oxide — determines rock hardness and color
Distinction between clastic (mechanical fragments) and non-clastic (chemical/organic) sedimentary rocks

concepts.name: Classification of Sedimentary Rocks: Clastic, Chemical, and Organic/Biogenic
key_dimensions: Clastic rocks by grain size: conglomerate > sandstone > siltstone > shale/mudstone — grain size sequence trap
Chemical sedimentary rocks: rock salt (halite), gypsum, chert — formed by evaporation or precipitation, not mechanical deposition
Organic/biogenic: coal (plant matter), limestone (marine organisms — coral/shells), chalk — UPSC trap on limestone origin
Limestone as both chemical and biogenic — ambiguity frequently exploited in questions

concepts.name: Sedimentary Rocks and Fossil Preservation: Significance and Conditions
key_dimensions: Why only sedimentary rocks preserve fossils: layered deposition, low heat/pressure, anoxic conditions — igneous and metamorphic destroy organic matter
Stratigraphic principle: older fossils in lower strata (Law of Superposition) — geological time scale linkage
Economic significance: petroleum and natural gas found in sedimentary basins (porous sandstone, limestone reservoirs)
India context: Gondwana coal deposits in sedimentary sequences of peninsular river valleys

concepts.name: Metamorphic Rocks: Types of Metamorphism — Contact, Regional, and Dynamic
key_dimensions: Contact (thermal) metamorphism: heat from igneous intrusion, localized effect, forms hornfels — no pressure component
Regional metamorphism: high T + high P over large areas, associated with mountain building (orogenesis) — most extensive type
Dynamic metamorphism: mechanical stress along fault zones, forms mylonite — least commonly tested but trap in advanced MCQs
UPSC trap: regional metamorphism ≠ contact metamorphism — scale, agent (pressure vs. heat), and product differ

concepts.name: Parent Rock (Protolith) to Metamorphic Rock Transformation Pairs
key_dimensions: Classic pairs: shale → slate → phyllite → schist → gneiss (progressive metamorphism sequence — grade matters)
Limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; coal → graphite/diamond — frequently tested conversions
UPSC trap: gneiss resembles granite visually but is metamorphic (foliated), not igneous — banded structure key distinction
Increasing metamorphic grade: index minerals (chlorite → biotite → garnet → staurolite → kyanite → sillimanite) — advanced but high-yield

concepts.name: Foliation and Non-Foliation in Metamorphic Rocks
key_dimensions: Foliated rocks: minerals align perpendicular to pressure — slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss (platy/banded texture)
Non-foliated rocks: marble, quartzite — formed under uniform pressure or from monomineralic protoliths
UPSC trap: marble is non-foliated metamorphic, not sedimentary — Taj Mahal marble linkage to Makrana, Rajasthan
Foliation vs. stratification (bedding in sedimentary) — visual similarity but different origin — common confusion point

concepts.name: Economic Importance of Rock Types: Minerals, Fuels, and Construction
key_dimensions: Igneous rocks: source of metallic minerals — iron ore (magnetite in basic igneous), copper, gold, chromite in ultramafic rocks
Sedimentary rocks: fossil fuels (coal, petroleum), evaporite minerals (gypsum, rock salt), iron ore (BIF — banded iron formations)
Metamorphic rocks: graphite, talc, asbestos, kyanite, marble, quartzite — industrial minerals
UPSC trap: diamond found in kimberlite (igneous ultramafic pipe) NOT metamorphic rocks, though graphite-to-diamond conversion is metamorphic concept

concepts.name: Deccan Traps: Formation, Composition, and Geomorphic Significance
key_dimensions: Origin: flood basalt volcanism during Late Cretaceous (~66 Ma), linked to Réunion hotspot — plate tectonics connection
Composition: basaltic lava flows forming layered trap topography — stepped landscape (trap = Dutch for stairs)
Black cotton soil (Regur): formed by weathering of basalt — high clay mineral content, water retention — agriculture linkage
Debate: Deccan volcanism and K-Pg mass extinction — UPSC contemporary science angle

concepts.name: Granite and Its Role in Peninsular India's Geomorphology
key_dimensions: Granite as plutonic igneous rock: coarse-grained, felsic, forms core of cratons and shields
Weathering of granite: produces tors, inselbergs, bornhardts — arid/semi-arid landform association
Chemical weathering of feldspar in granite → kaolinite (clay) — soil formation process
Gondwana connection: Peninsular India's Archaean granite-gneiss complex — oldest rocks in India context

concepts.name: Limestone: Formation, Types, and Karst Landform Association
key_dimensions: Formation: biochemical (coral/shell organisms) or chemical precipitation — marine environment origin
Solubility in weak carbonic acid → karst topography: sinkholes, caves, stalactites, stalagmites, dolines, poljes
Types: chalk (soft, porous), crystalline limestone, dolomite (Mg-rich) — dolomite more resistant to weathering
India examples: Meghalaya (Cherrapunji) karst caves, Vindhyan limestone — map-based relevance

concepts.name: Coal Formation: Carboniferous Sedimentary Process and Rank Sequence
key_dimensions: Formation: accumulation of plant matter in swampy conditions → peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite (increasing rank)
Rank = degree of coalification (carbon content increases, moisture/volatile matter decreases)
UPSC trap: anthracite is highest rank coal (highest carbon %), lignite is lowest — frequently reversed in options
Gondwana coalfields (Permian age) vs. Tertiary coalfields (Assam, NE India) — age and quality difference

concepts.name: Metamorphic Grade and Index Minerals: Barrovian Zones
key_dimensions: Concept of metamorphic zones defined by index minerals appearing at specific T/P conditions
Sequence from low to high grade: chlorite → biotite → garnet → staurolite → kyanite → sillimanite
Isograd: line connecting points of same metamorphic grade on geological map
UPSC trap: kyanite, andalusite, sillimanite are all Al₂SiO₅ polymorphs but form at different T/P — same chemistry, different conditions

concepts.name: Rocks and Soil Formation: Weathering Products and Parent Material Relationship
key_dimensions: Basalt → black cotton soil (Regur) in Deccan — high montmorillonite clay, swelling nature
Granite/gneiss → red and laterite soils in Peninsular India — iron oxide residue after leaching
Limestone → rendzina soils; sandstone → sandy, low-fertility soils
UPSC trap: laterite soil formed not just from basalt but from any rock under tropical humid conditions with intense leaching — parent rock ≠ sole determinant

concepts.name: Rocks as Aquifers: Porosity, Permeability, and Groundwater Storage
key_dimensions: Best aquifers: sandstone (primary porosity), limestone (secondary/karst porosity), alluvial gravel
Poor aquifers: granite and basalt (low primary porosity) BUT fractured/weathered basalt can hold water — UPSC trap
Confined vs. unconfined aquifers: impermeable shale/clay layers create artesian conditions
India relevance: hard rock aquifer challenges in Deccan plateau vs. alluvial aquifers in Indo-Gangetic Plain

concepts.name: Plate Tectonic Settings and Rock Type Association
key_dimensions: Divergent boundaries: basaltic igneous rocks (oceanic crust, mid-ocean ridge basalt — MORB)
Convergent boundaries: andesitic volcanism (subduction zones), regional metamorphism in collision zones, granite batholiths in continental crust
Transform boundaries: dynamic metamorphism (mylonite) along fault zones
UPSC trap: granite is NOT found at mid-ocean ridges (that's basalt) — granite is continental, basalt is oceanic crust composition

concepts.name: Banded Iron Formations (BIF) and Archaean Sedimentary Significance
key_dimensions: BIF: ancient chemical sedimentary rocks alternating iron oxide and chert layers — formed ~2.5 billion years ago
Significance: record of early Earth's oxygenation (Great Oxidation Event) — paleoenvironmental indicator
World's largest iron ore deposits (Pilbara, Australia; Jharkhand-Odisha belt, India) are BIF-derived
UPSC trap: BIF iron ore (hematite/magnetite) is sedimentary in origin, not igneous — contrasts with magmatic iron ore deposits
